title: I built random charts to find out if my strategy actually works (Part of it survived).
author: Money_Horror_2899
selftext:
On top of automated stuff, I also trade a discretionary strategy (structure, zones, divergences).

Last weekend, I finally tested it properly and I want to share the method, because I think most of us have never done this properly.

**Step 1: getting Claude to understand my strategy**

I had previously recorded videos about my discretionary method, so I took the transcripts (raw) of six of them and gave them to Claude Code (Fable).

It understood the whole logic in one shot and wrote the code for it. It even picked up rules I only mention once in passing.

**Step 2: checking it did not make things up**

I asked for a CSV of everything it detected. Every zone with its price range, every structure break with the date, every invalidation.

I checked it against my charts line by line. It was all correct: same zones, same breaks, same moments where a zone dies. That is when I trusted it and knew this was gonna be fun.

**Step 3: the fake markets**

Then it suggested something most people never think of: null tests.

Basically, it took all the real candles of my dataset, then kept every candle exactly as it is (same body and wicks), but shuffled them into a random order and rebuilt the chart.

The result looks like a realistic chart, but it has no memory. Nothing that happened before affects what comes next.

It gave me this analogy : "It is the sugar pill in a medical trial. If a drug cures 60 percent of patients that is great, unless a random sugar pill also cures 60 percent."

**Step 4: testing my entries against it**

It ran my entry rules on shuffled markets, up to 50 shuffles per test, then on the real markets I trade (NQ and BTC), and compared.

With the exact same exit rules applied to both markets, my setups produced 5 to 8 percentage points more winners on the real market than on the shuffled one, on every timeframe I tested. The biggest test simulated 18,000 trades.

So the entries genuinely find something and hold up against a control shuffle. That was a relief.

**Step 5: everything else**

Then it tested the rest, and this is where it got uncomfortable.

\- The stat most "structure" traders quote, that price continues about 60 percent of the time after a break of structure, showed up identically on the shuffled fake markets. So it comes from how the levels are drawn, not from a specific market behavior itself.

\- Every protective exit made things worse. Breakeven stops, partials at the first target, cutting on the first candle against you. All of them reduced expectancy. Turns out the version of my strategy with the highest expectancy was a set-and-forget approach.

\- My edge did not transfer as well to gold or S&P futures. Edges CAN BE specific to what you trade.

\- On the 20 biggest stocks, my version showed a profit that looked solid. But then the shuffled version on the same stocks made three times more. Basically, my discretionary strategy was capturing less than random clicking.

\- I even did some side quests throughout the chat: checking if zones weaken the more they are retested (spoiler: they DON'T), testing reversion trades after a sweep of the zones, etc.

**What I took away**

My entries are real on the markets I trade. My trade management was working against me and reduced expectancy.

For this session I had Claude Code plugged straight into my own market data infrastructure, but I am also building the Obside MCP so people can get asset search, price history, and backtesting without running the infra themselves. Disclosure: that one is my job.

To sum up, I was very pleasantly surprised to see how Claude can help not fall into the classic pitfalls and backtesting traps most people usually run into.

Happy to answer any questions about how the session went.
